city.name: Hue
summary: Hue was the capital of the Nguyen emperors from 1802 to 1945. On the north bank of the Perfume River stands their Citadel: a square of brick ramparts and moats about 2 km a side, with the walled Imperial City at its heart and quiet streets of garden houses round it. Across the river lies the newer town the French built, with the university, the hospital and the provincial offices.

In the early hours of 31 January 1968, during the Tet truce, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong troops took almost the whole city. Only the ARVN 1st Division headquarters at Mang Ca, in the Citadel's north corner, and the US advisers' MACV compound on the south bank held out. The NLF flag flew over the Citadel for 25 days.

US Marines cleared the south bank street by street; South Vietnamese troops and Marines then fought through the Citadel until the flag of South Vietnam went back up on 24 February. The battle ended on 2 March. About 5,800 civilians died, and mass graves later showed that at least 2,800 people had been executed during the occupation. Much of the city was left in ruins.
city.note: Streets are today's from OpenStreetMap, kept only inside the Citadel, on Gia Hoi island and in the south-bank town, all of which were built up by 1968. The river, moats and lakes are today's OpenStreetMap water. The Citadel walls, gates, palaces and temples use their OpenStreetMap outlines; the Flag Tower, MACV compound and south-bank offices are placed from the coordinates in Wikipedia's account of the battle and are approximate. Houses between the streets are generated. Map data (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL.

properties.name: Citadel walls
description: Brick ramparts about 6.6 m high and 20 m thick, 10 km round, built from 1805 for the emperor Gia Long in the Vauban style the French taught him, with 24 bastions, ten gates and a moat outside.

In 1968 the walls became the battlefield. Marines and South Vietnamese troops fought along the top of the east and south walls from 13 to 24 February, under fire from North Vietnamese troops dug into the towers and gatehouses.

properties.name: Imperial City
description: The emperors' walled palace city, about 600 m a side, ringed by its own moat. Inside lay the throne hall, the dynastic temples and the Purple Forbidden City, the emperor's private quarters.
Much of it burned in 1947, in the war against the French. In February 1968 North Vietnamese troops held it until the last days of the battle; South Vietnamese troops retook it on 24 February.

properties.name: Noon Gate (Ngo Mon)
description: The main gate of the Imperial City, built in 1833: a U-shaped stone and brick base with five passages, the centre one for the emperor alone, and the Five Phoenix Pavilion on top under yellow glazed tiles. Bao Dai abdicated here on 30 August 1945.
It came through the 1968 battle standing.

properties.name: Thai Hoa Palace
properties.description: The Hall of Supreme Harmony, the throne hall where the emperors held court, built in 1805 and rebuilt in 1833. It survived the fighting of 1947 and 1968.

properties.name: Thai Mieu
properties.description: A temple to the Nguyen lords who ruled before the dynasty took the imperial title.

properties.name: The To Mieu
properties.description: The dynastic temple of the Nguyen emperors, with altars to ten of them. The Nine Dynastic Urns stand in its courtyard.

properties.name: Phu Van Lau
properties.description: A two-storey pavilion of 1819 between the Flag Tower and the river, where royal edicts and the names of those who passed the court examinations were posted.

properties.name: Purple Forbidden City (ruins)
properties.description: The emperor's private palaces, open only to the royal family, eunuchs and maids. Most of its halls burned in February 1947, when the Viet Minh held the Citadel against the French; in 1968 only ruins and foundations remained.

properties.name: Flag Tower (Ky Dai)
description: A three-tier brick bastion of 1807 in the middle of the Citadel's river wall, carrying the flagpole of the capital. The present concrete pole dates from 1948.

At 08:00 on 31 January 1968 North Vietnamese troops raised the NLF flag here. It flew for 25 days, the symbol of their hold on Hue, until South Vietnamese troops hauled it down at 05:00 on 24 February and raised their own.

properties.name: Thuong Tu Gate
properties.description: The gate nearest the Truong Tien bridge. South Vietnamese troops tried to force it from the south in the first days of February 1968.

properties.name: Dong Ba Gate
properties.description: The east gate. North Vietnamese troops held its tower in February 1968. Marines took it on 15 February after six hours of fighting.

properties.name: Huu Gate
properties.description: The west gate. North Vietnamese troops left the Citadel through it and the Nha Do Gate at the end of the battle.

properties.name: Chanh Tay Gate
properties.description: The north-west gate, taken by North Vietnamese troops in the first hours of 31 January 1968.

properties.name: Mang Ca garrison
description: A fort in the north corner of the Citadel, garrisoned by the French in colonial times and in 1968 the headquarters of General Ngo Quang Truong's ARVN 1st Division. Its staff and a few hundred men held it against repeated assaults on 31 January, the only part of the Citadel the attackers never took.
From here South Vietnamese troops and, from 11 February, US Marines brought in by helicopter and boat fought south to retake the Citadel.

properties.name: Tay Loc airfield
properties.description: A small airstrip inside the Citadel. North Vietnamese troops overran it on 31 January 1968; its defenders slipped away to Mang Ca.

properties.name: Truong Tien Bridge
description: A steel bridge of six spans and 403 m, opened in 1900 and widened by the Eiffel company in 1939, the main link between the Citadel and the south-bank town.
Marines tried to cross it on 1 February 1968 and were driven back with heavy losses. North Vietnamese sappers dropped it on 7 February.

properties.name: Truong Tien Bridge (blown)
properties.description: North Vietnamese sappers dropped the bridge on 7 February 1968, cutting the old city off from the new. It was patched and rebuilt in the years after the war.

properties.name: Bach Ho railway bridge
properties.description: The railway bridge upstream of the Citadel. North Vietnamese sappers brought it down on the night of 1 to 2 February 1968.

properties.name: MACV compound
description: The compound of the US Military Assistance Command's advisers, a few hundred metres south of the river. Its advisers and guards held it when a North Vietnamese sapper company attacked on 31 January 1968.
Marines from Phu Bai fought their way in that afternoon, and it became the base for the battle for the south bank.

properties.name: Treasury
properties.description: The provincial treasury, taken by sappers on 31 January 1968. Marines stormed it on 4 February, blowing holes in its wall under cover of tear gas.

properties.name: Hue University
properties.description: The university at the south end of the Truong Tien bridge. Marines took it after three hours of room-to-room fighting in the first days of February 1968, and used it as their command post for the battle for the south bank.

properties.name: Thua Thien Provincial Headquarters
properties.description: The provincial government offices. Marines retook them on 6 February 1968 and raised the US flag, then took it down: the law allowed it only beside the South Vietnamese flag.

properties.name: Hue Central Hospital
properties.description: The city hospital, held by North Vietnamese troops until Marines retook it on 5 February 1968.

properties.name: Dong Ba market
properties.description: Hue's main market, on the river bank by the Gia Hoi bridge.

properties.name: Gia Hoi
properties.description: The old merchant quarter of shophouses east of the Citadel, settled by Chinese traders. The communist provisional government of Hue had its headquarters here from the start of the battle. South Vietnamese Rangers cleared it from 22 February 1968.

properties.name: Perfume River
properties.description: The Song Huong, which divides the old imperial city on the north bank from the newer town on the south. In 1968 the US Navy brought supplies up it by landing craft to a ramp near the MACV compound.
